newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices fall as supplies outstrip demand.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall as supplies outstrip demand.

text.p: Oil prices fell sharply on Wednesday under pressure from excess supplies of crude and fast growing refined product supply.
"The whole market is oversupplied with crude. Crude runs are high, so that only means more refined product is on its way," said Todd Miller, trader with Morgan Stanley.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange crude for July delivery finished 44 cents off at $18.79 a barrel while July gasoline settled a steep 1.70 cents off at 56.78 cents a gallon. July heating oil ended 1.01 cents a gallon lower at 51.44 cents.
Meanwhile, imports of gasoline are expected to be significant this summer.

"We may have several weeks where we fall to 350,000 to 400,000 barrels (per day) of gasoline imports but after that we will recover to higher levels for the rest of the summer," said Miller. Traders expect imports to recover to near or over 500,000 barrels per day after drifting lower short term.

Meanwhile, Tuesday evening's weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed record crude imports of 9.2 million barrels a day at a time when refinery utilization capacity stands at a torrid 97.6 percent.
The industry trade group said gasoline output was at a record 8.23 million barrels a day, pushing up gasoline stocks 1.7 million barrels. The data reflects the week ended June 13.
The API said stocks of reformulated gasoline, the grade deliverable against the NYMEX contract, rose a hefty three million barrels for the week.
Gold prices also fell sharply on news of more European central bank sales.

Belgian central bank officials said Wednesday the Belgian government proposed increasing the amount of central bank gold that can be sold as commemorative gold coins to 26 (metric) tons a year from 1999 onward, up to a maximum of 133 tons.

"The Belgian plan to sell more gold via a bullion coin issue still needs parliamentary approval and will not impact until 1999, but the market just saw it as more evidence of a trend toward central bank gold sales and ended weaker," said CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf.

Currently the National Bank of Belgium is authorised to sell up to 2.75 percent of its 1987 gold reserves in the form of coins, and the new proposal is to increase the amount authorised to 10 percent of the 1987 reserves.
At the start of 1987 the Belgian central bank held 1,329 (metric) tons of gold, but had sold 733 tons by the end of 1996.
The proposed extra sales of coins would allow Belgium to pay down more of its debt which stands at 129 pct of GDP, the highest debt-to-GDP ratio in the EU.
But the plan must still obtain parliamentary approval and would also be subject to approval by the new European Central Bank (ECB) which is due to be operational from January 1999.

"I dont believe the Belgian government will be able to sell that amount of gold in commemorative coins," said Leonard Kaplan, a broker with MONEX, one of the largest U.S. retailers of gold investment products.

Total world sales of major bullion coins (Krugerrand, American Eagle, Austrian Philharmonic, Canadian Maple Leaf, Australian Nugget, English Britannia) in 1996 amounted to 36.8 (metric) tons, according to the latest World Gold Council survey.
"But central banks are looking for a method of disposing of more of their gold reserves, so this kind of thing will only happen more often," Kaplan said.

The move by the Belgian government came only two days after Jean-Pierre Patat, an official of France's central bank, told the Financial Times gold conference in Prague that several European central banks which had sold gold from their reserves now feel there is no longer an advantage in doing so.
Belgium last sold a significant quantity of its reserves in March 1996 when it announced a sale of 203 tons.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $338.90/40, not far from the four year low around $336.15 seen on February 15 this year.
At New York's Commodity Exchange (COMEX) gold for August delivery ended down $2.80 at $341.00 an ounce, after seeing a new life-of-contract low at $340.60.
Soybean futures also tumbled on the Chicago Board of Trade as fund managers liquidated their long positions in the July contract following its recent extreme volatility.
"The funds came in this morning with the idea that they had to get out of July," said Jack Scoville, analyst with the Price Group in Chicago.
Soybeans for July delivery ended 20-1/2 cents lower at $8.32-1/2 a bushel.
"Volume's declining, trade is very choppy and it's flushing specs (speculatives) out of the market," said one veteran trader.
